Wealth, social capital, cultural capital, educational access, and even health outcomes are stratified and passed down along familial lines, creating rigid social castes before a child utters their first word. The state, as the dispassionate guardian of the collective good, possesses the scale, resources, and mandate to implement developmental protocols proven to maximize cognitive, emotional, and social potential – a level of consistent, high-quality input impossible for the vast majority of individual families to replicate.

Historical failures of state childcare (often in authoritarian contexts) stemmed from ideological dogma and resource scarcity, not the inherent concept. The true totalitarianism lies in perpetuating a system where a child's entire life trajectory is predetermined by the economic and social accident of their birth family.

To deny ectogenetic children this opportunity – to re-enslave them within the microcosms of privilege and disadvantage that fracture our societies – is a profound injustice. The purported benefits ignore 70+ years of developmental psychology proving that:
> Children need enduring, loving relationships with committed caregivers—not institutions or algorithms—to thrive.

While voluntary state support (e.g., parental leave, childcare subsidies) can enhance equality, forced separation from families is a hallmark of oppressive regimes. True equality comes from supporting families—not replacing them. Policies promoting this idea would:

  • Violate international human rights law,
  • Cause intergenerational trauma,
  • Undermine social fabric by destroying the primary unit of care: love.

For further reading:

This policy isn’t progressive—it’s a catastrophic regression to ideologies discredited by both science and history. 🌍✨

Ectogenesis—gestating humans in artificial wombs—would not merely add a new “option” to reproduction. It would shift the locus of the earliest, most vulnerable phase of human life from private bodies and private households to a deliberately designed, publicly mediated system. Once a society chooses to bring children into the world through a technology that is intrinsically institutional (labs, clinics, regulatory oversight, continuous monitoring), it must confront a second-order question: who should raise these children, and under what norms?

A compelling answer is state-controlled communal child-rearing for all ectogenetic children: a universal, non-family-based upbringing organized as a public good. Far from being dystopian, collective child-rearing can be the most equality-promoting, development-optimizing, and ethically coherent response to ectogenesis—precisely because it treats children as citizens-in-formation rather than as private property, and it replaces the lottery of birth circumstances with guaranteed conditions for flourishing.

1) Equality requires removing the “family lottery,” not merely regulating it

Modern societies claim to value equality of opportunity, yet they largely outsource childhood—arguably the primary determinant of life outcomes—to the private family. The result is predictable: wealth, education, social capital, neighborhood safety, nutrition, and exposure to stress vary dramatically from household to household. Even the best-intentioned parents cannot compensate for structural inequalities, and the state’s current patchwork of interventions (subsidies, schools, child welfare agencies) arrives late and unevenly.

Ectogenesis creates an opportunity to do what liberal democracies have always struggled to do: make the starting line genuinely fair. If a society can standardize the gestational environment—health monitoring, toxin avoidance, prenatal nutrition, early screening—it makes little sense to then hand infants into radically unequal postnatal environments and pretend the job is done. Equality is not achieved by ensuring identical births and unequal childhoods. A state-controlled communal system would guarantee baseline conditions that are known to shape lifelong trajectories: stable housing, consistent nutrition, access to medical care, low exposure to chronic stress, and high-quality early learning.

Most importantly, universal communal rearing avoids stigmatization. Programs targeted only at “at-risk” families often become underfunded, politically vulnerable, and socially marked. A universal system creates a shared institution with shared standards—like clean water or public vaccination—making it more durable and more just.

2) Children are persons with rights, not extensions of adult identity projects

Traditional family structures often operate—sometimes gently, sometimes harshly—as identity factories. Adults transmit religion, politics, language hierarchies, gender norms, and class expectations, and children absorb them long before they can evaluate them. This is not always malicious; it is simply what private households do. But if ectogenesis expands reproduction beyond biology—potentially allowing single individuals, corporations, or wealthy patrons to commission births—then the risk of children being treated as lifestyle accessories or ideological artifacts increases.

A communal system asserts a principle that becomes more urgent as reproduction becomes technologically mediated: children’s primary entitlement is to a developmentally sound upbringing, not to being claimed. The state, acting through transparent law and democratic oversight, is better positioned than any private household to guarantee certain non-negotiables: protection from abuse, access to education, freedom from exploitative labor, and exposure to a pluralistic set of adults and peers.

In other words, communal rearing is not anti-child; it is pro-child. It treats childhood as a protected phase of life with enforceable standards—rather than as whatever happens behind the closed doors of households of wildly varying competence and stability.

3) Communal rearing can optimize development by design, not by hope

The strongest empirical argument for communal child-rearing is not that “families are bad.” It is that child development is highly sensitive to quality, consistency, and resources—and a well-designed communal system can systematically provide them.

A universal communal model can be built around what developmental science repeatedly emphasizes:

  • Stable, reliable attachment relationships: Communal does not mean anonymous. It can mean small, consistent caregiving teams where each child forms secure bonds with a limited set of trained adults. Multiple attachment figures can be a strength, not a weakness, when stability is engineered rather than left to chance.
  • High caregiver training and accountability: Parenting is one of the most consequential tasks on earth and one of the least trained. A public system can professionalize early caregiving the way societies professionalize medicine and teaching—setting ratios, standards, ongoing education, and supervision.
  • Early detection and intervention: Speech delays, motor difficulties, hearing issues, neurodevelopmental differences, and trauma responses are often missed or addressed late. A communal system integrated with pediatric and developmental services can identify needs early and respond quickly.
  • Cognitively rich and emotionally safe environments: Language exposure, play-based learning, predictable routines, outdoor time, and arts access can be universal rather than dependent on zip code or parental time.
  • Reduced exposure to household-level stressors: Many harms to children come not from a lack of love, but from parental burnout, financial precarity, untreated mental illness, addiction, or domestic conflict. A communal model buffers children from these risk clusters by separating the child’s stability from adults’ private volatility.

Critics often assume the “family” is the gold standard, but in practice the modal experience is not an idealized household with abundant time and emotional regulation. It is a stressed household with limited resources. A competent communal system can outperform that median reality, not by replacing love with bureaucracy, but by ensuring love is backed by structure.

4) Collective upbringing promotes social cohesion and reduces caste formation

Ectogenesis could intensify stratification: those with resources might select genetic traits, purchase premium prenatal environments, or build exclusive child pipelines. If children then disperse into private family structures, the resulting society could harden into biologically and socially segregated strata—an inherited caste system with upgraded tools.

Universal communal rearing is a direct countermeasure. It forces cross-class, cross-cultural contact at the earliest stages of life, when social biases are most preventable and when empathy is most malleable. It builds a shared civic identity: children grow up alongside peers from diverse backgrounds in institutions that teach common rights and responsibilities. This is how you prevent “designer childhoods” from becoming the new mechanism of class reproduction.

The family, for all its intimacy, is also a powerful engine of in-group loyalty and out-group suspicion. Communal upbringing can widen the circle of belonging, making social solidarity a lived experience rather than an abstract ideal.

5) The state already bears responsibility—communal rearing simply makes that responsibility honest

Opponents will argue that state involvement invites overreach. But the state already intervenes heavily: it mandates schooling, vaccinates, regulates food and drugs, polices abuse, and funds child welfare systems when families fail. The status quo is not “private freedom” versus “state control”; it is pervasive state responsibility paired with inconsistent state capacity, arriving too late and often after harm has occurred.

Ectogenesis collapses the illusion that reproduction is purely private. When gestation itself is regulated and institutional, it becomes incoherent to insist that everything afterward must be privatized at all costs. A universal communal system is, in a sense, a consistency principle: if society collectively assumes responsibility for bringing children into the world through a shared technology, it should collectively assume responsibility for raising them to a fair, healthy baseline.

6) “Outside the family” need not mean “without family-like bonds”

A serious proposal for communal rearing should not pretend that children thrive on procedures alone. They thrive on belonging, continuity, and love. The case for communal child-rearing is strongest when it explicitly designs for those needs rather than dismissing them.

A state-controlled communal model can provide:

  • Small “home units” with consistent caregivers and a stable peer cohort.
  • Lifelong continuity records and enduring mentorship structures so children are not passed through faceless shifts.
  • Democratic oversight, independent auditing, and child advocacy offices to prevent institutional abuse and ensure transparency.
  • Structured roles for biological/genetic contributors (if any exist) that are optional, limited, and child-centered—more akin to mentorship or extended-community involvement than ownership.

The point is not to eliminate intimacy; it is to detach intimacy from private power. Children can have deep bonds without being positioned as someone’s possession.

Conclusion: Ectogenesis demands a new social contract, and communal rearing is the egalitarian choice

If ectogenesis becomes a pillar of reproduction, societies will be deciding—by default or by design—what childhood is for. Leaving ectogenetic children to be sorted into private households would reproduce the worst features of the current system: unequal starts, inconsistent caregiving quality, and the quiet conversion of children into vehicles for adult status and ideology. By contrast, state-controlled communal child-rearing treats childhood as a public good: universally protected, professionally supported, and oriented toward the child’s future autonomy.

Collective upbringing outside the traditional family structure is not a rejection of human connection. It is a commitment to distributing connection—along with safety, education, and opportunity—so that no child’s life chances depend on the happenstance of which adults claimed them. If ectogenesis represents a technological leap, communal rearing represents the moral one: an insistence that every child deserves not merely a safe gestation, but an equal and optimally nurturing start to life.
